network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network incorporates ten distinct, experimentally supported or plausible prebiotic pathways converging on L-alanine formation. The network includes Strecker (cyanohydrin/aldehyde), reductive amination and Bucherer–Bergs (keto-acid), thioester-sugar, and extraterrestrial delivery scenarios, modeling pyruvate as a hub intermediate for amino acid synthesis, and explicitly includes a final enantioenrichment module since all routes are racemic under primitive conditions. Each pathway is represented by documented, mineral-catalyzed or photochemical routes under hydrothermal and/or surface conditions, with convergence at either α-aminopropionitrile (Strecker) or pyruvate. A diversity of mineral agents is used where experimentally justified; environment allocation follows demonstrated or best-supported geochemical plausibility. The model accounts for environmental critiques, the concentration problem (especially for pyruvate) and incorporates key yield and selectivity constraints identified in the literature. All molecules are unique network nodes, and L-alanine itself arises by chiral amplification/separation from racemic alanine produced in earlier steps.

reactions.name: CO2 reduction and C–C bond assembly to pyruvate (Ni3Fe-catalyzed)

conditions.other: alkaline, H2 present; >5 mM NH3 not required

reactions.mechanism: CO2 hydrogenation and C–C coupling on awaruite; yields formate, acetate, then pyruvate at low µM concentrations.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated by Preiner et al. (2020, Nature Ecology & Evolution) and in Cody et al. (2000, Science), with awaruite mediating formation of pyruvate from CO2/H2. Pyruvate is generated in µM yields in hydrothermal conditions. Acetate is also produced as a byproduct. This provides a prebiotically plausible C3-ketoacid feedstock for amino acid synthesis. Yield is low and concentration requires local focusing (Preiner et al., 2020).

reactions.name: Pyruvate reductive amination to racemic alanine (FeS/Fe(OH)2)

conditions.other: alkaline (pH 9-10), high NH3 (>0.1 M for FeS route); 1:1 Fe(II):Fe(III) (green rust) for selectivity

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic attack of NH3 on pyruvate, forming iminopyruvate, which is reduced by the Fe(II) mineral to alanine; competing reduction to lactate.
reactions.reasoning: Solidly demonstrated (Huber & Wächtershäuser 2003; Barge et al. 2019, PNAS) with FeS, green rust, and Fe(OH)2 under alkaline, hydrothermal conditions. Supported by Kitadai et al. (2019, Science Advances). Selectivity is controlled by pH and Fe(II):Fe(III) ratio (Barge et al.).

reactions.name: Reductive amination of pyruvate (Ni0/H2 route)

conditions.other: pH 7-8; can operate at only 6 mM ammonia

reactions.mechanism: Pyruvate is aminated by NH3, reduced by H2 on Ni0 to racemic alanine; lactate forms as parallel reduction.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Kaur et al. (2024, Chem), who show up to 18–40% alanine yield with 5–15% lactate. The route is robust at modest NH3 concentrations, improving prebiotic plausibility. Meteorite metals also work (Aletai meteorite, Kaur et al.).

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs synthesis from pyruvate (cyanide-ammonia-CO2)
reactions.mechanism: Pyruvate reacts with NH3, HCN, and CO2 to form hydantoin and then undergoes ring opening to racemic alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated in Pulletikurti et al. (2022, Nature Chem.), with pyruvate plus cyanide, ammonia and CO2 giving high-yield α-amino acids. The intermediate is hydantoin. The necessity of providing both pyruvate and cyanide in the same locale is a practical challenge (Pulletikurti et al, critique).

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis: cyanohydrin/aldehyde pathway (classical Strecker)

conditions.other: can run on evaporitic surfaces, post-spark discharge

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation from acetaldehyde and ammonia, nucleophilic addition of HCN to imine forming α-aminopropionitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Classical Strecker pathway, demonstrated since Miller (1953, Science) and widely reviewed (Johnson et al. 2008, Science). Acetaldehyde can be atmospheric or photochemical in origin (Miller–Urey), HCN from discharge or photo-oxidation. Cited by Patel et al. (2015, Nature Chem.), Sutherland’s cyanosulfidic variants.

reactions.name: α-aminopropionitrile hydrolysis to racemic alanine

conditions.other: acidic to neutral pH; wet-dry cycling promotes hydrolysis

reactions.mechanism: Acid/base-catalyzed hydration of the nitrile followed by tautomerization and ammonia elimination to give alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker hydrolysis step is universally demonstrated, both neat and clay-catalyzed. The reaction proceeds under plausible surface conditions. Cited by Bada (Mètode), Johnson et al. (2008), and Sutherland (2015).

reactions.name: Photoreduction of HCN to acetaldehyde via cyanosulfidic protometabolism
reactions.mechanism: Reductive homologation of HCN to C2–C3 aldehydes, photochemically, mediated by copper and hydrogen sulfide.
reactions.reasoning: Explicitly shown in Patel et al. (2015, Nature Chem.), Ranjan et al. (arXiv), and further characterized in Sutherland's work. This provides a geochemically plausible and photochemically robust bridge between HCN-rich settings and Strecker substrates.

reactions.name: Formose-type condensation: formaldehyde + glycolaldehyde to glyceraldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Aldol condensations and isomerizations of formaldehyde and glycolaldehyde, giving glyceraldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Well-known prebiotic C3-sugar formation (Weber 1985, J. Mol. Evol.; also Benson & Calvin, historical). Borate minerals stabilize and steer selectivity. Provides a sugar intermediate for further chemistry. Used as input for the thiol-catalyzed pathway.

reactions.name: Thiol-assisted amination of glyceraldehyde to alanine (Weber route)
reactions.mechanism: Glyceraldehyde dehydrates to methylglyoxal, reacts with ammonia and thiol, via hemithioacetal and imine, then to alanine and lactate.
reactions.reasoning: Thiol-catalyzed amino acid synthesis is demonstrated by Weber (1985, 1998); although yield is low, the route is robust and does not require HCN. Provides both alanine and lactate. The thiol must be locally available (Weber, 1998 OLEB).

reactions.name: Transamination: pyruvate to alanine swap with amino acid nitrogen donor
reactions.mechanism: Pyridoxal forms a Schiff base with amino acid, facilitating amino group transfer to pyruvate to yield alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Non-enzymatic transamination demonstrated with pyridoxal and metal ions (Dherbassy et al. 2023, JACS; Life 2023; Kaur et al. 2024). Boosts yield at low NH3; pyridoxal’s own prebiotic synthesis is unsolved, but its catalytic properties are well established in laboratory analogs.

reactions.name: Extraterrestrial delivery: racemic alanine import from meteorites/parent body
reactions.mechanism: Amino acid delivery by meteorite infall or incorporation from planetesimal-derived organics.
reactions.reasoning: Directly confirmed by Murchison (Engel & Macko 1997, Nature; Pizzarello & Cronin 1998) and Bennu samples (Glavin et al. 2025, Nature Astronomy). Delivered alanine is always racemic, with only questionable natural excess in rare samples.

reactions.name: Chiral amplification/separation to L-alanine

conditions.catalyst: cir. polarized UV, mineral surface, or other
conditions.other: drying interfaces, repeated cycling, or asymmetric irradiation

reactions.mechanism: Minor L/D excess through asymmetric UV photolysis, selective adsorption/crystallization or templating, followed by physical separation and amplification.
reactions.reasoning: No demonstrated route gives L-alanine exclusively (see Engel & Macko 1997; Meinert et al. 2014; Modica et al. 2014; Glavin et al. 2021/2025). Chiral amplification or separation is required. %L-enantiomer excess can be generated by CPL (1–5%), crystallization, etc., but always incomplete and depends on local cycles. Included for network completeness (see 'homochirality' reviews, e.g. Modica et al. 2014, ApJ).

pathways.name: Hydrothermal CO2 → pyruvate → alanine (FeS, Fe(OH)2 route)
pathways.description: CO2 fixed on Ni3Fe forms pyruvate, then reductive amination to alanine via FeS or Fe(OH)2 minerals.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal CO2 → pyruvate → alanine (Ni0/H2 route)
pathways.description: As above, but pyruvate amination and reduction is catalyzed by Ni0 and H2 for enhanced selectivity at low NH3.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal CO2 → pyruvate → alanine (pyridoxal/metal-aided transamination)
pathways.description: Pyruvate, formed hydrothermally, is aminated via pyridoxal and Fe(III)/Al(III) catalysis to alanine.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal CO2 → pyruvate → alanine (Bucherer–Bergs with cyanide input)
pathways.description: Hydrothermal pyruvate reacts with surface-supplied cyanide, ammonia, and CO2 in the Bucherer–Bergs pathway.

pathways.name: Strecker-cyanide photoredox cascade (HCN photoreduction + Strecker)
pathways.description: HCN is photoreduced to acetaldehyde (cyanosulfidic), which enters classical Strecker synthesis with HCN and ammonia.

pathways.name: Surface Strecker from primordial aldehyde atmospheres
pathways.description: Preformed acetaldehyde (from atmospheric photolysis or discharge) reacts in Strecker sequence to form alanine.

pathways.name: Bucherer–Bergs: surface-supplied pyruvate or imported pyruvate (parent body)
pathways.description: Pyruvate accumulates by other means (HCN homologation, delivery, or CO2 surface fixation) and undergoes Bucherer–Bergs synthesis.

pathways.name: Formose–thiol route (Weber) from formaldehyde, glycolaldehyde, ammonia, thiol
pathways.description: C1/C2 feedstocks assembled to sugars, aminated by thiol-catalyzed condensation to alanine.

pathways.name: Extraterrestrial delivery (meteoritic parent-body formation)
pathways.description: Alanine delivered already formed from meteorites, incorporated into prebiotic inventory.

pathways.name: Formose–aldehyde–ammonia condensation (parent body/surface, HCN-free)
pathways.description: Amino acids (including alanine) synthesized by condensation of formaldehyde, aldehydes, and ammonia at high temperature (asteroid/planetesimal scenario).

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway (CO2 → pyruvate → alanine via FeS/Fe(OH)2) is strongly aligned with literature and best understood experimentally. However, its mass balance is problematic: both rxn_001 (CO2 + H2 → pyruvate + acetate) and rxn_002 (pyruvate + NH3 → alanine + lactate) are systemically unbalanced in C, H, and O. As the structure is sound but reaction balancing is absent or faulty, the score is penalized for chemical feasibility. Hydrothermal conditions and mineral catalysts are appropriate and supported by experiment. The final chiral enrichment step is well-justified.
suggestions: Fix major atom-balance errors: add water or CO2 as byproducts where balancing analysis suggests.
Provide explicit reaction stoichiometries.
Verify all molecules are represented with correct formulas/InChI.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrothermal CO2 → pyruvate → alanine via Ni0/H2 is a direct analog of recent experiments (Kaur et al.). Reaction conditions and catalysts are appropriate, but both rxn_001 and rxn_003 are unbalanced for C, H, and O. Network logic mirrors top-tier literature but is penalized for major mass conservation violations.
suggestions: Balance all reactions; add H2O or CO2 where required.
Provide explicit coefficients and check all reactants/products for accurate formulas.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrothermal transamination from pyruvate is plausible and experimentally supported (notably when pyridoxal and metal ions are present), but rxn_001 and rxn_010 reactions are not balanced. Otherwise, the logical steps and environmental assignments are robust. Chiral amplification step is correctly included.
suggestions: Balance reaction equations and check for missing byproducts.
Clarify pyridoxal/metal cofactor requirements if claimed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Bucherer–Bergs route from pyruvate is fully described in recent literature and does support prebiotic alanine synthesis. Rxn_004 is balanceable, but rxn_001 is still C, H, O unbalanced, so minor penalty. Surface/aqueous conditions align with experiment. Both logic and convergence with modern metabolic-like pathways are strengths.
suggestions: Balance all reactions, especially in upstream pyruvate synthesis.
Explicitly define all small-molecule byproducts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Strecker/HCN photoredox cascade aligns with Sutherland's cyanosulfidic networks, but multiple steps are elementally unbalanced (notably rxn_007 and rxn_006). HCN photoreduction to acetaldehyde, as written, is not chemically balanced (and literature usually routes through intermediate sugars). The Strecker step is otherwise known and feasible. The pathway is realistic but must fix the stoichiometry.
suggestions: Balance all reactions for mass and charge.
Clarify intermediates in HCN photoreduction.
Explicitly track water/ammonia losses in aminonitrile hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Classical Strecker synthesis from aldehyde atmospheres is textbook prebiotic chemistry. However, as shown, the key aminonitrile hydrolysis (rxn_006) is unbalanced, as is the aldehyde/HCN/NH3 condensation. Mechanistically sound but in need of explicit stoichiometry and byproduct tracking.
suggestions: Balance all reactions and provide water/other byproduct stoichiometry explicitly.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the most direct and chemically sound version: Bucherer–Bergs from imported or surface pyruvate. All steps are (at least potentially) balanceable and supported by experiment (Krishnamurthy et al.). Conditions are environmentally plausible, and the chiral step is required and present. Only minor clarification of stoichiometry may remain, but the pathway is superior due to its simplicity and alignment with known chemistry.
suggestions: Provide explicit stoichiometric coefficients for Bucherer–Bergs reaction.
Ensure all intermediate structures/formulas are accurate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Weber formose–thiol pathway is experimentally shown. The formose condensation (rxn_008) is likely sound, but the thiol-assisted amination (rxn_009) is not atom-balanced (extra H, N, S). Further, the presence and prebiotic fate of 3-mercaptopropionic acid should be explicitly tracked. The path matches the literature but requires reaction balancing and attention to catalyst sources.
suggestions: Explicitly balance all reactions.
Clarify the fate of the thiol.
Verify molecular structures/formulas.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Extraterrestrial delivery of racemic alanine is fully supported by meteorite returns (Murchison, Bennu). Since no chemistry is performed in rxn_011 (import), atom/charge balance is not applicable. The enantioenrichment step is again required and present. The pathway is accurate, if not terrestrial, and all environmental assumptions hold.
suggestions: No changes needed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pathway is plausible: formose reactions feed aldehydes into Strecker-type or ammonia condensation routes, but as written, rxn_005 and rxn_006 are unbalanced for atom numbers. The route matches credible scenarios (Kebukawa, Koga), especially for asteroidal/parent body settings, but technical improvements to balancing and intermediates are needed.
suggestions: Balance all reactions.
Provide water and ammonia as explicit byproducts as needed.

evaluation.network_feedback: This synthesis network for L-alanine covers the full range of prebiotic routes and explicitly acknowledges all major experimental and environmental constraints from the literature. Pathway diversity and environmental realism are strengths, as is the explicit enantioenrichment step—a necessity since all feedstock routes yield racemic alanine. However, a majority of routes contain reactions that are not atom- or charge-balanced, which must be corrected for a fully valid network. The best pathway is extraterrestrial delivery (P9), as it is atomistically trivial and perfectly supported by sample data. Of the prebiotic synthesis routes, the Bucherer-Bergs path (P7) is the most immediately viable and least problematic. To reach 'excellent' status (>0.9 overall), upstream and aminating/reduction reactions must each be explicitly mass/charge balanced per the deterministic check. Overall, the network mirrors literature not only in route diversity but also in capturing the domain's main mechanistic caveats and is recommended with revision.
